title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — mors animae not from commination
pass_a_gloss: Nothing can be answered, except that indeed bodily and eternal death was not inflicted on him, but yet the death of the soul placed in privation of righteousness was inflicted. But against this I press thus. If the death of the soul was inflicted on him, for that reason it was inflicted on him, because the threat required it. But it was not for that reason inflicted on him, because the threat required it. Therefore that death was not inflicted on him. The major cannot be denied. I prove the minor. If for that reason the death of the soul was inflicted on him, because the threat required it, then also bodily and eternal death were inflicted on him, because the threat required this no less. Yet these deaths were not inflicted on him. Therefore the death of the soul is not for that reason inflicted on him, because the threat required it. About the minor there can be no dispute. The major, though openly true, is yet confirmed by this, that God had threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual. If therefore God's truth and justice required that this be inflicted on Adam that day, the same truth and justice required no less that those deaths also be inflicted the same day; the reason, as you see, is equal. What would be suited to dissolving this argumentation I notice nothing of in the Learned Man's reply.
pass_b_english: The only way out is to say: bodily and eternal death were not laid on him, yet the soul's death—privation of righteousness—was. I press against that. If the soul's death was laid on him, it was laid on him because the threat required it. But it was not laid on him because the threat required it. So that death was not laid on him.

The major stands. For the minor: if the soul's death was laid on him because the threat required it, then bodily and eternal death were laid on him too, for the threat required those no less. Yet those deaths were not laid on him. So the soul's death was not laid on him because the threat required it. The minor is beyond dispute. The major, already plain, is confirmed because God had threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual. If God's truth and justice required the spiritual death that day, the same truth and justice required those other deaths the same day—the reason is the same. I see nothing in the Learned Man's reply that dissolves this.
source_text: Nihil potest responderi, nisi, ei quidem inflictam non fuisse mortem corporis & aeternam, sed tamen inflictam fuisse mortem animae positam in privatione justitiae. Sed contra sic insto. Si inflicta ei fuit mors animae, ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Sed non ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Ergo ei inflicta mors illa non fuit. Major negari non potest. Minorem probo. Si ideo ei inflicta fuit mors animae, quia id exigebat comminatio, etiam ei inflictae fuerunt mors corporis & aeterna, quia hoc non minus exigebat comminatio. Attamen hae mortes non sunt ei inflictae. Ergo mors animae non est ideo ei inflicta, quia id exigebat comminatio. De minore nulla lis esse potest. Major, quanquam aperte vera est, tamen eo confirmatur, quod non minus mortem corporis & aeternam Deus comminatus fuerat quam spiritualem. Haec igitur si Dei veritas, & justitia exigebant ut eo die Adamo infligeretur, eadem, veritas & justitia, non minus exigebant, ut illae etiam mortes infligerentur eadem die; par, uti vides, ratio est. Quod huic argumentationi dissolvendae accommodatum sit, nihil animadverto in responsione Viri Docti.

choices.choice: soul-death not from threat; else bodily+eternal same day
